query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replace a portion of the heavy Hf in HfMoTaTiZr with a lightweight element—specifically, substitute roughly 10 atomic percent Hf with aluminum—to lower the overall density yet preserve the high‐temperature and room‐temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr, which forms a single-phase BCC solid solution with high strength at room temperature and around 1000 °C but a relatively high density (~10.21 g/cm³).
generation.intervention: Substitute approximately 10 at% of Hf with Al (resulting in an alloy composition that may be described as AlMoTaTiZr), keeping the other alloying elements unchanged.
generation.conditions: Mechanical loading (tensile and compressive) at room temperature and at elevated temperatures around 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The alloy’s overall phase (a single-phase BCC solid solution) is maintained by the added Al; the lattice distortion induced by the light Al atoms helps in retaining solid solution strengthening while reducing average atomic mass.
generation.mechanism: By replacing a heavy element (Hf) with a low-density element (Al), the average density decreases while the formation of a homogeneous BCC phase is preserved through solid solution effects. This keeps strength and high-temperature stability intact. A similar concept has been demonstrated in other HEAs where low-density elements like Al have been used to tailor mechanical and thermal performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to exhibit a visibly lower density (targeting at least a 5–10% reduction) relative to the as-cast alloy while maintaining or only slightly modifying yield strength and ductility at both room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties and density of the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy as reported.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to service conditions from room temperature up to approximately 1000 °C under standard tensile and compressive loads relevant for structural and aerospace applications.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise percentage of Al that can be added without inducing unwanted phase transformations or brittle intermetallic formation. Additionally, the exact retention of high-temperature mechanical properties may require fine-tuning of the substitution level.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize the proposed Al-substituted alloy (AlMoTaTiZr) using arc-melting or casting, ensuring homogeneous mixing. Fabricate test samples and perform a series of mechanical tests (tensile and compression) at room temperature and at around 1000 °C. Use X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) to confirm the presence of a single-phase BCC structure without deleterious intermetallic phases.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile/compressive strength at room temperature and at ~1000 °C
Ductility measures (e.g., elongation to failure, fracture toughness)
Phase analysis (via XRD) and microstructural observations (via SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-substituted alloy fails to show a density reduction of at least 5% relative to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, or if the yield strength (or ductility) at either room temperature or at ~1000 °C is reduced by more than 10% compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is rejected.

Microstructure, Tensile and Creep Properties of Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 High Entropy Alloy

Abstract: This paper examines the microstructure and mechanical properties of Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20. Two casting processes, namely, gravity casting and suction-assisted casting, were applied, both followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP). The aim of the current study was to investigate the creep and tensile properties of the material, since the literature review revealed no data whatsoever regarding these properties. The main findings are that the HIP process is responsible for the appearance of a Hexagonal Close Packed (HCP) phase that is dispersed differently in these two castings. The HIP process also led to a considerable increase in the mechanical properties of both materials under compression, with values found to be higher than those reported in the literature. Contrary to the compression properties, both materials were found to be highly brittle under tension, either during room temperature tension tests or creep tests conducted at 282 °C. Fractography yielded brittle fracture without any evidence of plastic deformation prior to fracture.

How 10 at% Al Addition in the Ti-V-Zr-Nb High-Entropy Alloy Changes Hydrogen Sorption Properties

Abstract: Al0.10Ti0.30V0.25Zr0.10Nb0.25 was prepared to evaluate the effect of 10% aluminum into the previously reported quaternary alloy, Ti0.325V0.275Zr0.125Nb0.275. The as-cast quinary alloy formed a single-phase body centered cubic solid solution and transformed into a body centered tetragonal after hydrogenation. The alloy had a storage capacity of 1.6 H/M (2.6 wt.%) with fast absorption kinetics at room temperature, reaching full capacity within the first 10 min. The major improvements of Al addition (10%) were related to the desorption and cycling properties of the material. The temperature for hydrogen release was significantly decreased by around 100 °C, and the quinary alloy showed superior cycling stability and higher reversible storage capacity than its quaternary counterpart, 94% and 85% of their respective initial capacity, after 20 hydrogenation cycles without phase decomposition.
